title: Panja Sahib, 1922
hookLine: Sikhs lay on the railway to stop a train and feed the prisoners on it; two died

cards: Pots of dal and stacks of rotis, still warm, wrapped in cloth on a railway platform.
The people who cooked them have heard that a train is coming through their town, carrying Sikh prisoners arrested at Guru ka Bagh to a distant jail. The cooks want to feed them.
The station master says the train isn't scheduled to stop here. So what do you do with a langar that has nowhere to go?

teach.b: The town is Hasan Abdal, and its gurdwara is Panja Sahib. Sikh tradition tells that Guru Nanak rested there, and that a rock rolled down the hill toward him was stopped by his open hand, which left its print in the stone.
Panja means the outstretched hand, and pilgrims still touch that print.

teach.h: THE SANGAT LAY ON THE RAILS.
teach.b: When the request to stop was refused, members of the sangat went down onto the rails and lay across them, in the path of the train.
Histories of the reform movement say the train ran over some of them before it came to a halt. Two men, Bhai Karam Singh and Bhai Partap Singh, died of their injuries. The train had stopped.

teach.h: THE FOOD WENT THROUGH THE WINDOWS.
teach.b: The food was handed through the windows, and the prisoners ate. It wasn't done to block anyone or to win an argument; it was done so that hungry people could eat.

teach.h: EARN, AND GIVE WITH YOUR HAND.
teach.b: At Ang 1245 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak says that the one who earns by honest work and gives some of it away with their own hand has recognized the way. The langar is that teaching made into a kitchen.

At Panja Sahib, a town cooked for strangers, then put their own bodies between the meal and the timetable. The place had long been remembered for one open hand. After that day, it was remembered for many.

how: Sikhs remember the saka of Panja Sahib alongside the gurdwara's older story of Guru Nanak's handprint; pilgrims to Hasan Abdal touch the print in the stone, and the two men who died on the rails are honored as shaheeds.

games.q: you've cooked for prisoners on a passing train, and you're told it won't stop. what does the sangat do?
o: give the food away to the town instead.
lie across the rails so the train has to stop.
games.why: they lay across the rails. the train ran over some before it halted, two men died, and the prisoners were fed through the windows.

practice: Rest one hand on your knee, palm up, fingers spread, the way the panja is pictured, and breathe slowly.

Bring to mind someone who might be hungry today, a neighbor, a coworker skipping lunch, a stranger you pass, and think of one thing you could actually hand them. If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Panja Sahib. The gurdwara of the handprint at Hasan Abdal, where the sangat lay on the rails to stop a train and feed the prisoners on it. Today's word.

orig.note: panja, the outstretched hand; sahib, a title of honor for a sacred place.

carryVoice: Your line: they stopped the train. A meal mattered that much. Day nine hundred eighty-eight.
